reminder: The ruin probability $\psi(u)$ is the probability that the capital of an insurer, started at $u$, ever falls below zero.
definition: For a risk process $R_t=u+ct-S_t$, as in the [Cramér–Lundberg model](c:cramer-lundberg-model), the ruin time is the [stopping time](c:stopping-time) $\tau(u)=\inf\{t\ge0:R_t<0\}$, and the (infinite-horizon) ruin probability is $\psi(u)=P(\tau(u)<\infty)$ for initial capital $u\ge0$. The finite-horizon ruin probability is $\psi(u,T)=P(\tau(u)\le T)$. Equivalently, $\psi(u)=P(\sup_{t\ge0}(S_t-ct)>u)$.
examples: For exponential claims with mean $\mu$ and $c>\lambda\mu$, $\psi(u)=\frac{\lambda\mu}{c}\exp(-(\frac1\mu-\frac\lambda c)u)$.
With $\lambda=1$, $\mu=1$ and $c=2$, this gives $\psi(0)=1/2$ and $\psi(u)=\frac12e^{-u/2}$.
Under the net profit condition $c>\lambda\mu$, $\psi(0)=\lambda\mu/c$ for every claim size law.
Non-example: $P(R_T<0)$ at one fixed time $T$ is not the ruin probability, because the capital can fall below zero before $T$ and recover by time $T$.

reminder: A self-avoiding walk is a nearest-neighbor path on a lattice that never visits the same vertex twice.
definition: An $n$-step self-avoiding walk on a [graph](c:graph) $G$ from a vertex $x$ is a sequence of vertices $(\omega_0,\dots,\omega_n)$ with $\omega_0=x$, with $\omega_{i-1}\omega_i$ an edge for each $i$, and with $\omega_i\ne\omega_j$ for $i\ne j$. Let $c_n$ be the number of such walks. The uniform measure on them is a model of a linear polymer, usually on $\mathbb Z^d$.
examples: On $\mathbb Z^2$ from the origin, $c_1=4$, $c_2=12$, $c_3=36$ and $c_4=100$.
On $\mathbb Z$, $c_n=2$ for every $n\ge1$, because the walk must go straight to the left or to the right.
Non-example: the walk $(0,0),(1,0),(0,0)$ on $\mathbb Z^2$ is a [random walk](c:random-walk) path but not self-avoiding, because it visits $(0,0)$ twice.

steps: In graph theory, a path is a walk whose vertices are all distinct.
An $n$-step self-avoiding walk from $x$ is a path with $n$ edges that starts at $x$.
The probabilistic model adds the uniform measure on these paths for each $n$.
links.why: It shows that self-avoiding walks are the paths of graph theory, studied as random objects.

reminder: A process whose law is unchanged when time is scaled by b and space by b^H.
definition: A [stochastic process](c:stochastic-process) $X$ is $H$-self-similar if, for every $b > 0$, the process $(X(bt))_{t \ge 0}$ has the same finite-dimensional distributions as $(b^H X(t))_{t \ge 0}$. The number $H$ is the Hurst index.
examples: [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) is self-similar with $H = 1/2$.
A strictly $\alpha$-stable Lévy process is self-similar with $H = 1/\alpha$.
Non-example: a Poisson process is not self-similar, because $N(bt)$ takes integer values while $b^H N(t)$ does not.

reminder: A semimartingale is a local martingale plus an adapted process of finite variation.
definition: An adapted [càdlàg](c:is-cadlag) process $X$ is a semimartingale when $X_t=X_0+M_t+A_t$, where $M$ is a [local martingale](c:local-martingale) with $M_0=0$ and $A$ is an adapted càdlàg process with $A_0=0$ whose paths have [bounded variation](c:bounded-variation) on every bounded interval. The decomposition is not unique in general, but a continuous $X$ has exactly one decomposition with continuous $M$ and $A$. By the Bichteler–Dellacherie theorem, the semimartingales are exactly the good integrators for stochastic integrals.
examples: [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) is a continuous semimartingale with $M=B$ and $A=0$.
An Itô process $X_t=X_0+\int_0^tb_s\,ds+\int_0^t\sigma_s\,dB_s$ is a semimartingale.
Every [Lévy process](c:levy-process) is a semimartingale, by the Lévy–Itô decomposition.
Non-example: fractional Brownian motion with Hurst index $H\ne1/2$ is not a semimartingale.

steps: Let $M$ be a [local martingale](c:local-martingale).
Choose the finite variation part $A=0$.
Then $M=M_0+(M-M_0)+A$ is a semimartingale decomposition.
links.why: It shows that semimartingales add a finite variation drift to local martingales, so that Itô's formula treats both together.

steps: Write a [Lévy process](c:levy-process) by the Lévy–Itô decomposition as $X_t=bt+\sigma B_t+J_t+M_t$.
Here $J_t$ is the sum of the jumps of size above $1$, finitely many on each bounded interval, so $J$ has finite variation.
The compensated sum $M_t$ of the jumps of size at most $1$ is a square-integrable martingale.
So $X=(\sigma B+M)+(bt+J)$ is a local martingale plus a process of finite variation.
links.why: It shows that all of stochastic calculus for semimartingales applies to Lévy processes.

reminder: A slowly varying function $L$ satisfies $L(\lambda x)/L(x)\to1$ as $x\to\infty$ for every $\lambda>0$.
definition: A positive [measurable function](c:measurable-function) $L$ on $(0,\infty)$ is slowly varying at infinity when $\lim_{x\to\infty}L(\lambda x)/L(x)=1$ for every $\lambda>0$. Equivalently, $L$ is a [regularly varying function](c:regularly-varying-function) of index $0$. Such an $L$ changes more slowly than every power: $x^{-\varepsilon}L(x)\to0$ and $x^{\varepsilon}L(x)\to\infty$ for every $\varepsilon>0$.
examples: Every positive function with a positive finite limit at infinity, such as a constant, is slowly varying.
The functions $\log x$, $\log\log x$ and $\exp(\sqrt{\log x})$ are slowly varying.
Non-example: $L(x)=x^{0.1}$ is not slowly varying, because $L(2x)/L(x)=2^{0.1}\ne1$.
Non-example: $L(x)=2+\sin(\log x)$ is bounded but not slowly varying, because with $\lambda=e^{\pi/2}$ the ratio is $(2+\cos t)/(2+\sin t)$ with $t=\log x$, which has no limit.

steps: Start from a [regularly varying function](c:regularly-varying-function) $f$ with $f(\lambda x)/f(x)\to\lambda^\rho$ for every $\lambda>0$.
Take the index $\rho=0$.
Then the limit is $\lambda^0=1$, which is the definition of slow variation.
links.why: It places slowly varying functions inside the regularly varying class, as the factor $L$ in $f(x)=x^\rho L(x)$.

reminder: The spontaneous magnetization $m^*(\beta)=\lim_{h\downarrow0}\langle\sigma_0\rangle_{\beta,h}$ is the magnetization that remains when the external field vanishes.
definition: For the [Ising model](c:ising-model) on $\mathbb Z^d$ at [inverse temperature](c:inverse-temperature) $\beta$, the spontaneous magnetization is $m^*(\beta)=\lim_{h\downarrow0}\langle\sigma_0\rangle_{\beta,h}$, where $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\beta,h}$ is the infinite-volume state in the field $h>0$. It equals $\langle\sigma_0\rangle^+_\beta$, the [expected value](c:expected-value) of the spin at the origin under the plus Gibbs measure at $h=0$, and also the right derivative $\partial\psi/\partial h(\beta,0^+)$ of the pressure. For $d\ge2$, $m^*(\beta)=0$ for $\beta\le\beta_c$ and $m^*(\beta)>0$ for $\beta>\beta_c$.
examples: On $\mathbb Z^2$, Yang's formula gives $m^*(\beta)=(1-\sinh(2\beta)^{-4})^{1/8}$ for $\beta>\beta_c$.
In the [Curie–Weiss model](c:curie-weiss-model) with $\beta>1$, $m^*(\beta)$ is the positive solution of $m=\tanh(\beta m)$.
Non-example: the one-dimensional Ising model has $m^*(\beta)=0$ for every $\beta$, because $\langle\sigma_0\rangle_{\beta,h}=\sinh h/\sqrt{\sinh^2h+e^{-4\beta}}$ tends to $0$ as $h\downarrow0$.

steps: A correlation function of a spin model is an expectation $\langle\prod_{x\in A}\sigma_x\rangle$ of a product of spins.
Take the plus Gibbs measure at $h=0$ and the one-point set $A=\{0\}$.
This one-point function $\langle\sigma_0\rangle^+_\beta$ is the spontaneous magnetization $m^*(\beta)$.
links.why: It shows that the order parameter of the Ising model is its simplest correlation function under the plus boundary condition.

reminder: A stable law keeps its type under sums: a sum of iid copies is an affine image of one copy.
definition: A nondegenerate law $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is stable when for every $n\ge1$ there are $a_n>0$ and $b_n\in\mathbb{R}$ such that, for [iid random variables](c:iid-random-variables) $X,X_1,\dots,X_n$ with law $\mu$, the sum $X_1+\dots+X_n$ has the law of $a_nX+b_n$. Then $a_n=n^{1/\alpha}$ for an index $\alpha\in(0,2]$, and the index $\alpha=2$ gives the normal laws. The stable laws are exactly the nondegenerate limits in distribution of affinely normalized sums of iid random variables.
examples: The [normal distribution](c:normal-distribution) is stable with $\alpha=2$, because a sum of $n$ iid standard normal variables has the law of $\sqrt nX$.
The Cauchy law with density $1/(\pi(1+x^2))$ is stable with $\alpha=1$, because the mean $(X_1+\dots+X_n)/n$ is again standard Cauchy.
The Lévy law with density $(2\pi)^{-1/2}x^{-3/2}e^{-1/(2x)}$ on $(0,\infty)$, the law of the hitting time of level $1$ by Brownian motion, is stable with $\alpha=1/2$.
Non-example: the Poisson law is not stable, because a sum of iid Poisson variables is Poisson with a larger mean, which is not an affine image of the original law.

steps: Let $\mu$ be stable, so that $X_1+\dots+X_n$ has the law of $a_nX+b_n$.
Solve for $X$, which then has the law of $\sum_{i\le n}(X_i-b_n/n)/a_n$, a sum of $n$ iid terms.
This holds for every $n$, so $\mu$ is an [infinitely divisible distribution](c:infinitely-divisible-distribution).
links.why: It lets the Lévy–Khintchine formula describe stable laws, with a Lévy measure proportional to $|x|^{-1-\alpha}$ on each half line when $\alpha<2$.

steps: Take the index $\alpha=2$.
The stable laws with $\alpha=2$ have the characteristic functions $\exp(imt-\sigma^2t^2/2)$.
These are the [normal distributions](c:normal-distribution) $N(m,\sigma^2)$, with $a_n=\sqrt n$ and $b_n=(n-\sqrt n)m$.
links.why: It shows that the normal law is the only stable law with finite variance, and that all other stable laws have heavy power tails.

reminder: A stationary distribution $\pi$ of a Markov chain satisfies $\pi P=\pi$, so a chain started from $\pi$ keeps law $\pi$.
definition: A stationary distribution of a [Markov kernel](c:markov-kernel) $P$ on a state space $S$ is a [probability measure](c:probability-measure) $\pi$ on $S$ with $\pi P=\pi$, that is, $\int\pi(dx)P(x,A)=\pi(A)$ for every measurable set $A$. On a countable space this reads $\sum_x\pi(x)P(x,y)=\pi(y)$ for every $y$. If $X_0$ has law $\pi$, then every $X_n$ of the [Markov chain](c:markov-chain) has law $\pi$.
examples: For simple [random walk](c:random-walk) on a finite connected graph, $\pi(x)=\deg(x)/(2|E|)$ is stationary.
For the two-state chain with $P(1,2)=a$ and $P(2,1)=b$, where $a+b>0$, the stationary distribution is $\pi=(b/(a+b),\,a/(a+b))$.
Non-example: simple random walk on $\mathbb Z$ has no stationary distribution. Every invariant measure is a constant multiple of counting measure, so it has infinite total mass.

steps: An invariant measure for a Markov kernel $P$ is a measure $\mu$ with $\mu P=\mu$.
Add the condition that $\mu$ has total mass $1$.
Then $\mu$ is a stationary distribution of $P$.
links.why: It shows that a stationary distribution is a normalized invariant measure, so it exists only when some invariant measure has finite mass.

steps: Suppose that $\pi(x)P(x,y)=\pi(y)P(y,x)$ for all states $x,y$.
Sum both sides over $x$.
Since $\sum_xP(y,x)=1$, this gives $\sum_x\pi(x)P(x,y)=\pi(y)$.
So a distribution in detailed balance is stationary.
links.why: It shows that detailed balance is a sufficient local condition for stationarity, which is how reversible chains are built.

reminder: A stationary sequence has joint laws that do not change when you shift time.
definition: A sequence $(X_n)_{n\ge0}$ of [random variables](c:random-variable) is (strictly) stationary when the shifted sequence $(X_{n+k})_{n\ge0}$ has the same law as $(X_n)_{n\ge0}$ for every $k\ge0$. Equivalently, every [finite-dimensional distribution](c:finite-dimensional-distribution) is invariant under time shift: $(X_{n_1+k},\dots,X_{n_m+k})$ has the law of $(X_{n_1},\dots,X_{n_m})$ for all indices $n_1,\dots,n_m$ and all $k\ge0$.
examples: Every sequence of [iid random variables](c:iid-random-variables) is stationary.
A [Markov chain](c:markov-chain) started from a [stationary distribution](c:stationary-distribution) $\pi$, with $\pi P=\pi$, is a stationary sequence.
The moving average $X_n=Z_n+cZ_{n-1}$ of iid $Z_n$ is stationary, and for $c\ne0$ its terms are not independent.
Non-example: the simple symmetric [random walk](c:random-walk) $S_n$ is not stationary, because $\mathrm{Var}(S_n)=n$ changes with $n$.

steps: A [stationary process](c:stationary-process) $(X_t)_{t\in T}$ has finite-dimensional laws that are invariant under the shifts $t\mapsto t+s$ of the time set.
Take the time set $T=\mathbb{N}$ or $T=\mathbb{Z}$ with integer shifts.
The process is then a sequence $(X_n)$ whose law is invariant under $n\mapsto n+k$, which is a stationary sequence.
links.why: It shows that a stationary sequence is the discrete-time case of a stationary process, so ergodic theory for the shift applies to it.

steps: Let $X_1,X_2,\dots$ be [iid random variables](c:iid-random-variables) with law $\mu$.
The joint law of $(X_{1+k},\dots,X_{m+k})$ is the product measure $\mu^{\otimes m}$, which does not depend on $k$.
So every iid sequence is stationary, while stationarity also allows dependence between the terms.
links.why: It shows that stationarity keeps the time invariance of iid sequences but drops their independence.

reminder: The stochastic exponential $\mathcal{E}(X)$ solves $dZ=Z\,dX$ with $Z_0=1$, the analogue of the exponential for semimartingales.
definition: For a [semimartingale](c:semimartingale) $X$, the stochastic (Doléans-Dade) exponential $\mathcal{E}(X)$ is the unique semimartingale $Z$ with $Z_t=1+\int_0^tZ_{s-}\,dX_s$, an equation for a [stochastic integral](c:stochastic-integral). For continuous $X$ it is $\mathcal{E}(X)_t=\exp(X_t-X_0-\frac12\langle X\rangle_t)$, where $\langle X\rangle$ is the [quadratic variation](c:quadratic-variation). If $X$ is a continuous local martingale, then $\mathcal{E}(X)$ is a positive local martingale.
examples: For $X=\sigma B$ with a Brownian motion $B$, $\mathcal{E}(\sigma B)_t=\exp(\sigma B_t-\sigma^2t/2)$, a positive martingale with mean $1$.
For $X_t=\mu t+\sigma B_t$, $\mathcal{E}(X)_t=\exp(\sigma B_t+(\mu-\sigma^2/2)t)$, the geometric Brownian motion of the Black–Scholes model.
For a [Poisson process](c:poisson-process) $N$, $\mathcal{E}(N)_t=2^{N_t}$, because each jump multiplies $Z$ by $1+\Delta N=2$.
Non-example: $\exp(B_t)$ is not $\mathcal{E}(B)$, because Itô's formula gives $d\exp(B_t)=\exp(B_t)\,(dB_t+\frac12dt)$.

steps: Let $X_t=at$ for a real constant $a$.
This $X$ is continuous with finite variation, so $\langle X\rangle=0$.
The equation $Z_t=1+\int_0^taZ_s\,ds$ then has the solution $Z_t=e^{at}$.
So the stochastic exponential of a deterministic linear path is the ordinary [exponential function](c:exponential-function).
links.why: It shows that, for continuous $X$, the correction term $-\frac12\langle X\rangle$ is the only change from the ordinary exponential.

reminder: A strong solution of a stochastic differential equation is built from the given Brownian motion and initial value alone.
definition: Fix a probability space with a [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) $B$, an initial value $\xi$ independent of $B$, and the [filtration](c:filtration) $(\mathcal{F}_t)$ that $\xi$ and $B$ generate, augmented by the null sets. A strong solution of the [stochastic differential equation](c:stochastic-differential-equation) $dX_t=b(t,X_t)\,dt+\sigma(t,X_t)\,dB_t$ with $X_0=\xi$ is a continuous process $X$ adapted to $(\mathcal{F}_t)$ such that both integrals exist and $X_t=\xi+\int_0^tb(s,X_s)\,ds+\int_0^t\sigma(s,X_s)\,dB_s$ for all $t$, almost surely. A weak solution, in contrast, can use a Brownian motion and a filtration that are constructed together with $X$.
examples: If $b$ and $\sigma$ are Lipschitz in $x$ uniformly in $t$ and have linear growth, a unique strong solution exists, by Picard iteration.
The equation $dX_t=\mu X_t\,dt+\sigma X_t\,dB_t$ has the strong solution $X_t=X_0\exp(\sigma B_t+(\mu-\sigma^2/2)t)$.
The Ornstein–Uhlenbeck equation $dX_t=-\theta X_t\,dt+\sigma\,dB_t$ has the strong solution $X_t=e^{-\theta t}X_0+\sigma\int_0^te^{-\theta(t-s)}\,dB_s$.
Non-example: Tanaka's equation $dX_t=\operatorname{sgn}(X_t)\,dB_t$ with $X_0=0$ has weak solutions but no strong solution.

steps: Take $\sigma=0$, so that the equation becomes the [ordinary differential equation](c:ordinary-differential-equation) $x'(t)=b(t,x(t))$ with $x(0)=\xi$.
If this initial value problem has a unique solution for each start, the solution is a measurable function of $\xi$ and $t$.
So $x(t)$ is measurable for $\sigma(\xi)\subseteq\mathcal{F}_t$, and $x$ is a strong solution.
links.why: It shows that a strong solution extends the classical solution of an initial value problem to equations driven by a given noise path.

reminder: For a subexponential distribution, a sum of independent copies is large mainly because one summand is large.
definition: A [distribution function](c:distribution-function) $F$ on $[0,\infty)$ with $F(x)<1$ for all $x$ is subexponential when $\overline{F^{*2}}(x)/\overline F(x)\to2$ as $x\to\infty$, where $\overline F=1-F$ and $F^{*2}$ is the [convolution](c:convolution) of $F$ with itself. Then, for [iid random variables](c:iid-random-variables) $X_i$ with distribution function $F$ and every $n\ge2$, $P(X_1+\dots+X_n>x)\sim nP(X_1>x)\sim P(\max_{i\le n}X_i>x)$ as $x\to\infty$.
examples: A Pareto law with $\overline F(x)=x^{-\alpha}$ for $x\ge1$ is subexponential, and so is every law on $[0,\infty)$ with a [regularly varying](c:regularly-varying-function) tail.
The lognormal law and the Weibull law with $\overline F(x)=e^{-x^\beta}$ and $0<\beta<1$ are subexponential.

Non-example: the [exponential distribution](c:exponential-distribution) with rate $\lambda$ is not subexponential, because $\overline{F^{*2}}(x)=(1+\lambda x)e^{-\lambda x}$, so the ratio $1+\lambda x$ tends to $\infty$.

steps: Let $F$ be subexponential with tail $\overline F=1-F$.
A standard lemma gives $\overline F(x-y)/\overline F(x)\to1$ for every fixed $y>0$, so $F$ is long-tailed.
A long tail decays more slowly than every exponential, so $e^{\varepsilon x}\overline F(x)\to\infty$ for each $\varepsilon>0$.
Hence $E[e^{\varepsilon X}]=\infty$ for every $\varepsilon>0$, and $F$ is a [heavy-tailed distribution](c:heavy-tailed-distribution).
links.why: It shows that subexponential laws form a large class of heavy-tailed laws, the class where the single big jump principle holds.

reminder: A supermartingale is an adapted integrable process whose conditional mean of the next value is at most the present value.
definition: An adapted process $(X_n)$ of [integrable](c:integrable-function) random variables for a [filtration](c:filtration) $(\mathcal{F}_n)$ is a supermartingale when the [conditional expectation](c:conditional-expectation) satisfies $\mathbb{E}[X_{n+1}\mid\mathcal{F}_n]\le X_n$ almost surely for every $n$. In continuous time the condition is $\mathbb{E}[X_t\mid\mathcal{F}_s]\le X_s$ for $s\le t$. So a supermartingale decreases on average, and $-X$ is a submartingale.
examples: The fortune in a game that is unfavourable to the player, $X_n=\xi_1+\dots+\xi_n$ with independent integrable steps of mean at most $0$, is a supermartingale.
If $f$ is a finite excessive function for a [Markov chain](c:markov-chain) $(Y_n)$ and $\mathbb{E}[f(Y_0)]<\infty$, then $f(Y_n)$ is a nonnegative supermartingale.
Every [martingale](c:martingale) is a supermartingale.
Non-example: a simple random walk with $P(\xi_i=1)=2/3$ is not a supermartingale, because $\mathbb{E}[X_{n+1}\mid\mathcal{F}_n]=X_n+1/3>X_n$.

steps: Let $(X_n)$ be a [martingale](c:martingale), so $\mathbb{E}[X_{n+1}\mid\mathcal{F}_n]=X_n$.
Equality implies the inequality $\mathbb{E}[X_{n+1}\mid\mathcal{F}_n]\le X_n$, so $(X_n)$ is a supermartingale.
A process is a martingale exactly when it is both a supermartingale and a submartingale.
links.why: It shows that results for supermartingales, such as the convergence of nonnegative supermartingales, apply to martingales.

reminder: A triangular array has rows of random variables that are independent within each row, with row lengths that grow.
definition: A triangular array is a family of real [random variables](c:random-variable) $X_{n,k}$, $n\ge1$, $1\le k\le k_n$, with $k_n\to\infty$, such that for each $n$ the variables $X_{n,1},\dots,X_{n,k_n}$ of row $n$ are [independent](c:independent-random-variables). Variables in different rows can be dependent, and they can live on different probability spaces. Limit theorems for arrays describe the row sums $S_n=X_{n,1}+\dots+X_{n,k_n}$.
examples: For iid $X_k$ with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2\in(0,\infty)$, the array $X_{n,k}=(X_k-\mu)/(\sigma\sqrt n)$, $k\le n$, has row sums that converge in distribution to the standard normal law.
For Bernoulli variables $X_{n,k}$ with $P(X_{n,k}=1)=\lambda/n$, $k\le n$, the row sums are binomial and converge in distribution to the Poisson law with mean $\lambda$.
The Lindeberg–Feller theorem gives normal limits for the row sums of triangular arrays under the Lindeberg condition.
Non-example: $X_{n,k}=Y/n$ for $k\le n$, with one random variable $Y$, is not a triangular array in this sense, because the terms of a row are not independent unless $Y$ is constant.

steps: Start with one sequence of [iid random variables](c:iid-random-variables) $X_1,X_2,\dots$ with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2\in(0,\infty)$.
Set $X_{n,k}=(X_k-\mu)/(\sigma\sqrt n)$ for $1\le k\le n$.
Each row is independent, so this is a triangular array with $k_n=n$.
The Lindeberg–Feller theorem for this array gives the classical central limit theorem.
links.why: It shows that arrays let the law of the summands change with $n$, which gives Poisson limits as well as normal limits.

reminder: The von Neumann entropy $-\operatorname{tr}\rho\log\rho$ measures the uncertainty in a quantum state $\rho$.
definition: For a [density matrix](c:density-matrix) $\rho$ on $\mathbb{C}^d$, which is positive semidefinite with trace $1$, the von Neumann entropy is $S(\rho)=-\operatorname{tr}(\rho\log\rho)$, with the [matrix logarithm](c:matrix-logarithm) and the convention $0\log0=0$. If $\rho$ has the [eigenvalues](c:eigenvalue) $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_d$, then $S(\rho)=-\sum_i\lambda_i\log\lambda_i$, the Shannon [entropy](c:entropy) of the spectrum. It satisfies $0\le S(\rho)\le\log d$, and $S(\rho)=0$ exactly for pure states.
examples: A [pure state](c:pure-state) $\rho=|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|$ has the eigenvalues $1,0,\dots,0$ and entropy $0$.
The maximally mixed state $\rho=I/d$ has entropy $\log d$, the largest value on $\mathbb{C}^d$.
For a Bell state of two qubits, each reduced density matrix is $I/2$, so its entropy is $\log2$, one bit of entanglement.
Non-example: the diagonal entries of $\rho$ in a fixed basis do not give $S(\rho)$ in general: for $\rho=|+\rangle\langle+|$ the diagonal is $(1/2,1/2)$ with Shannon entropy $\log2$, but $S(\rho)=0$.

steps: Let $p=(p_1,\dots,p_d)$ be a probability vector and $\rho=\operatorname{diag}(p_1,\dots,p_d)$.
This $\rho$ is a density matrix, and $\rho\log\rho=\operatorname{diag}(p_1\log p_1,\dots,p_d\log p_d)$.
So $S(\rho)=-\sum_ip_i\log p_i$, the Shannon [entropy](c:entropy) of $p$.
links.why: It shows that von Neumann entropy reduces to Shannon entropy on diagonal, classical states.

steps: Let $|\psi\rangle$ be a pure state of a bipartite system $A\otimes B$.
Its reduced state $\rho_A=\operatorname{tr}_B|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|$ is a density matrix on $A$.
The [entanglement entropy](c:entanglement-entropy) of $|\psi\rangle$ is $S(\rho_A)$, the von Neumann entropy of this reduced state.
It is $0$ exactly when $|\psi\rangle$ is a product state.
links.why: It shows that entanglement entropy is the von Neumann entropy of a subsystem of a pure state.
